titolo: Why America Got Rich While Canada Fell Behind
descrizione:
Canada and the United States share the longest border on Earth, a language, and legal roots from Britain. In 1980 Canadians were almost as rich as Americans. Today the gap is wide, and one province is now poorer per person than most US states. What happened?

We follow the money: weak competition, thin investment in machines, talent leaving for Silicon Valley and Seattle, oil sold to one buyer, and a housing boom that swallowed more capital than every factory and software program combined. The lesson reaches far beyond Canada.

scene.testo: A border where a nation fell behind its twin. Banks nobody dares to shake up. Houses that swallowed everything. So why did Canada slip?
Same language, same laws, twin economies. How did one pull away?
Two countries share the longest border on Earth, the same language, laws inherited from Britain, and more natural resources than almost anyone.
For most of the last century, they looked like twins. In 2011, measured in dollars, the average Canadian actually out-produced the average American.
Today, in those same dollars, Canada produces about as much per person as Mississippi, America's poorest state.
The Bank of Canada itself has called it an emergency. So how did two countries with the same start end up this far apart?

eventi.testo: Central bank calls it an emergency

scene.testo: The answer runs through bankers in Toronto, oil in Alberta, a coder in Vancouver, and one thing almost nobody in Canada wants to fix.
That 2011 number was an illusion. The Canadian dollar was strong, and oil was selling for close to one hundred dollars a barrel.
When oil crashed in 2014, the illusion went with it. Measured by what money really buys, the story is slower and clearer.
In 1980, Canadians were about 95 percent as rich as Americans. For years after 2000, about 83. Today, about three quarters.
And on the map, it gets worse. Ontario, the country's economic engine, is now poorer per person than 43 US states.
Quebec beats just one, Mississippi. Put all 60 states and provinces on one board, and seven of the bottom ten are Canadian.

eventi.testo: Seven of bottom ten are Canadian

scene.testo: Even Alberta, the oil province, slid from seventh place in 1999 to twenty-fifth. Same board, same start.
Here's the strange part. Canada is the most educated country in the OECD. Almost two in three adults hold a college degree.
And yet every hour a Canadian works produces about 71 cents for every American dollar. In 1984, it was 88.
Since 2000, Canadian productivity has grown about eight tenths of a percent a year, less than half the American pace.
In March 2024, the Bank of Canada's number two told business leaders in Halifax, it's an emergency, time to break the glass.
The problem isn't the workers. It's what they're given to work with. For every dollar of new capital an American gets, a Canadian gets 55 cents.
For machinery alone, it's 41 cents. In 2007, firms on both sides invested almost the same per worker.
By 2024, American companies were investing nearly twice as much per worker. Better educated workers, worse equipped.
So why aren't Canadian companies buying the machines? To see why, look at who a Canadian company actually has to fight.
Often, not many. Six banks hold 94 percent of all banking assets in the country, and came through 2008 without a single failure.
But safe and dominant also means little pressure to bet on new companies. Two airlines control about 80 percent of domestic flying.
In 1986, Canada had at least eight separately owned grocery chains. Five of them were bought by rivals.
For years, three companies took about nine in ten mobile phone dollars. Even provinces trade behind barriers, with different rules at every line.
The IMF estimated that removing those internal barriers could make Canadians about four percent richer. And when profits are protected, nobody needs a new machine.
South of the border, it works the other way. In 2024, American startups raised over 200 billion dollars in venture capital.
That is roughly four times more per head than in Canada. Most of those bets fail, but the few that win build entire industries.

eventi.testo: Most bets fail, winners build industries

scene.testo: So a lot of Canada's best talent follows the money. One study found two thirds of software engineering graduates from top programs had left for America.
Canada's own statistics agency found computer science and math graduates are the most likely to stop filing taxes at home within three years.

eventi.testo: Coders are the likeliest to leave

scene.testo: You can see why. In Seattle, the typical software developer earns about 167,000 dollars a year.
Drive 230 kilometers north to Vancouver, and a software engineer earns about 95,000. Down in San Francisco, it's closer to 187,000.
Hold on to that number. We'll come back to what that Vancouver engineer pays for a house.
Canada did build giants. In 2000, Nortel was worth about a third of the entire Toronto stock market.
In 2009, BlackBerry sold a fifth of the world's smartphones. Both collapsed, and nothing that big replaced them.
Without rivals forcing them to change, the companies that stayed big were the protected ones. So where was Canada's money going?
Canada sits on one of the largest oil reserves on Earth. In 2024, it pumped a record five million barrels a day, mostly from Alberta.
Energy is Canada's biggest export, about a quarter of all goods it sells abroad. That came to roughly 195 billion Canadian dollars in 2024.
And about 93 percent of the crude it exports goes to one customer, the United States.
Having one customer is dangerous. In November 2018, without enough pipelines to reach anyone else, Alberta's heavy crude sold for just 13 dollars a barrel.
That was 43 dollars less than American oil. Alberta had to order producers to cut output just to stop the price falling further.
Oil can make a country rich. It doesn't make it productive. An hour of work in Alberta produces almost twice as much as in Nova Scotia.

eventi.testo: Oil, not machines, explains the gap

scene.testo: After the oil crash of 2015, the stock of machinery per Canadian worker actually shrank. On research, Canada spends about half the American share.
But oil isn't where most of Canada's money went. The biggest pile went somewhere much closer to home.
In 2021, something happened that never had before. According to the Bank of Montreal, Canada put more money into housing than into every factory, machine, and piece of software combined.
At that peak, housing took over ten percent of the economy, more than America at the height of its own bubble.
It wasn't one year. From 2018 to 2023, Canada spent a bigger share of its economy on homes than any of 35 advanced economies, about twice the American share.
Houses are bought with borrowed money. Canadian households owe about one dollar seventy-six for every dollar they earn after tax.
At the 2022 peak, it was almost one ninety. Mortgages make up about three quarters of it.
For a bank, a mortgage is safer than a loan to a new company. So Canadian banks lend far more to home buyers than to businesses.
Now back to our engineer in Vancouver. In Seattle, a software developer's salary buys a typical house in under six years.
In Vancouver, the same kind of house costs nearly 14 years of pay. He earns less and pays more.
And the young are being pushed out. Among Canadians in their late twenties, home ownership fell from 44 to 36 percent in just ten years.
Which brings us to the problem hardly anyone dares to fix. Two in three Canadian households own their home.
Nearly half of all household wealth in Canada is the house itself. In America, it's about a quarter.
Make houses cheaper, and you make most homeowners poorer, at least on paper. So prices stay high, and money stays in houses instead of factories.
So is Canada doomed? Not quite. Canadians live about three years longer, and are around two and a half times less likely to be murdered.

eventi.testo: Canada wins on life and safety

scene.testo: It also carries one of the lowest net public debts in the G7, and its income is shared more evenly than in America.
But the trend is hard to ignore. In 2021, the OECD projected Canadian living standards would grow more slowly over 40 years than any other member.
Here is a number few expect: Canada has about four times more land per person than America, and far more beneath it.
So why did two neighbors who started level drift so far apart? Not because of the land.
It was because of where the money went. None of it is fixed by geography, and the IMF's four percent from free trade between provinces is still on the table.

eventi.testo: Free internal trade is still unused

scene.testo: America sent its capital into machines, software, and risky new companies, and made them fight each other.
Canada sent much of its capital into protected companies, oil it could sell to only one buyer, and houses.
That's the warning for every rich country. When owning things pays more than building things, the building slows down.
